At the left-sympathetic end, *The Atlantic* profiles "The Woman Who Has Prevented 200 Executions," casting an anti-death-penalty advocate in explicit hero terms — the word "prevented" frames executions as harms stopped rather than sentences not carried out. Several outlets occupy the center: NPR notes that "public opinion on death penalty is split," *The Free Press* poses the open philosophical question "Can an Execution Be Ethical?," and a second *Atlantic* piece takes a detached historical angle on "How Botched Executions Were Handled in Centuries Past." At the right end, *The Federalist* takes the sharpest rhetorical stance, deriding "Generals And Journos Who Cheered Endless Wars" for being "Squeamish On Live Executions" — language designed to mock critics of public execution as hypocritical rather than to examine the policy question neutrally.

stories.topicLabel: DOJ sues California over election and immigration policies
stories.analysis: Coverage of the DOJ's lawsuit against California over election and immigration policies was largely uniform across these three outlets, with a bias spread of just 0.5 points separating the most left-leaning from the most right-leaning headline. Most framing was descriptive and restrained: NPR's headline aggregated the story neutrally alongside other news using plain explanatory language ("why the DOJ is suing California"), while the Los Angeles Times offered mild skepticism of the proceedings without targeting either side, characterizing the dispute through process-focused language like "Big assertions, sharp exchanges, little clarity." The modest outlier was Reason, whose headline — "Trump Loses Yet Another Sanctuary City Case" — introduced cumulative language ("Yet Another") that implies a pattern of administration legal setbacks, representing the only notable departure from neutral framing. Even so, the differences across outlets were minor, and no headline adopted strongly ideological language favoring either California or the federal government.
